title: THE LESSON I LEARNED FROM BARNABAS’ INFLUENCE
paragraphs: THE LESSON I LEARNED FROM BARNABAS’ INFLUENCE
Some people change your life without ever standing behind a pulpit.
They never write a bestselling book.
They never become famous.
History barely remembers their voice.
Yet entire generations are transformed because they chose to believe in someone everyone else had already given up on.
That is the lesson I learned from Barnabas.
And if we miss it, we may miss one of the most powerful pictures of the Gospel hidden in the pages of Scripture.
The Kingdom of God has always been filled with Peters, Pauls, Davids, and Moseses—names that echo through centuries.
But behind many of those names stands a Barnabas.
A quiet believer.
A faithful encourager.
A bridge builder.
A man who understood something that many Christians still struggle to grasp today:
God sees people according to who they can become through grace, not merely according to who they have been through sin.
That truth changed the early church.
And it can change us too.
The first time we meet Barnabas, his name is actually Joseph.
Acts 4:36 tells us:
“Joseph, a Levite from Cyprus, whom the apostles called Barnabas (which means Son of Encouragement).”
The Greek text uses the name Βαρναβᾶς (Barnabas), which Luke explains as “Son of Encouragement.”
The word translated encouragement comes from the idea of παράκλησις (paraklēsis), meaning comfort, exhortation, strengthening, consolation, and coming alongside someone to help them continue forward.
Barnabas was not merely a positive thinker.
He was a lifter of weary souls.
A strength-giver.
A man who reflected the heart of Christ.
While many seek influence by being noticed, Barnabas became influential by helping others become who God called them to be.
That is a different kind of greatness.
One day a former terrorist arrived in Jerusalem.
His name was Saul.
Before becoming the Apostle Paul, Saul had spent his life hunting Christians.
Acts 8:3 says he was ravaging the church.
The Greek word is ἐλυμαίνετο (elymaineto), describing brutal destruction.
Families feared him.
Believers hid from him.
His reputation was soaked in scandal.
Then Jesus intervened.
On the road to Damascus, everything changed.
The persecutor became a disciple.
The destroyer became a preacher.
The enemy became family.
But there was one problem.
Nobody believed him.
Can you blame them?
Imagine hearing that the man responsible for imprisoning Christians suddenly wanted to join your Bible study.
Trust does not rebuild overnight.
The church was terrified.
Acts 9:26 says:
“When he came to Jerusalem, he tried to join the disciples, but they were all afraid of him, not believing that he really was a disciple.”
Notice what happened next.
Barnabas stepped forward.
Not Peter.
Not James.
Not John.
Barnabas.
Acts 9:27:
“But Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles.”
One sentence.
Yet that sentence changed Christian history.
Barnabas became the bridge between Saul’s past and God’s future.
Everyone else saw a scandal.
Barnabas saw grace.
Everyone else saw danger.
Barnabas saw transformation.
Everyone else saw what Saul had done.
Barnabas saw what Jesus had done.
That is one of the greatest lessons I have ever learned.
Many people claim to believe in grace until grace shows up wearing the face of someone they do not trust.
The Gospel is easy to celebrate when it transforms people we already like.
It becomes harder when God starts rewriting the story of someone whose past still makes us uncomfortable.
Yet this is exactly what Jesus does.
The Gospel is not a self-improvement program.
It is a resurrection story.
Paul would later write:
The Greek says:

καινὴ κτίσις
(kainē ktisis)
A new creation.
Not repaired.
Not patched.
Not modified.
New.
Barnabas believed that.
Not as a theological slogan.
As a living reality.
And because he believed it, Paul eventually became one of the most influential apostles in history.
Think about that.
Humanly speaking, Christianity as we know it looks dramatically different without Paul's ministry.
Yet one reason Paul's ministry survived its earliest days was because one man chose to believe God's grace was bigger than someone's reputation.
How many future Pauls are waiting for a Barnabas?
How many broken people remain trapped because nobody will risk believing Jesus can truly change them?
How many prodigals never find their footing because believers keep introducing them to their past instead of introducing them to their future in Christ?
The story becomes even more powerful later.
Acts 11 describes revival breaking out in Antioch.
The church sends Barnabas to investigate.
What did he do when he arrived?
He celebrated.
Acts 11:23 says:
“When he arrived and saw what the grace of God had done, he was glad and encouraged them all.”
Again we see encouragement.
Again we see Barnabas strengthening others.
Again we see a man whose first instinct was not criticism but recognition of God's work.
Barnabas understood something many believers forget.
You cannot constantly remind people of their failures and simultaneously expect them to walk confidently into God's calling.
Grace does not ignore sin.
Grace defeats sin through transformation.
The Hebrew Scriptures reveal this same pattern repeatedly.
The word often translated grace is חֵן (chen).
It describes favor freely given.
Undeserved kindness.
A gift that originates in the character of God rather than the worthiness of the recipient.
From Genesis to Revelation, God repeatedly writes redemption where humanity expected rejection.
Abraham lied.
Jacob deceived.
Moses killed.
David committed adultery.
Peter denied Christ.
Paul persecuted believers.
Yet God continued writing.
The enemy specializes in labels.
God specializes in redemption.
The enemy says, “This is who you were.”
Jesus says, “Watch who I am making you become.”
That is the heartbeat of our theme:
Barnabas understood that long before it became a slogan.
He lived it.
Then came another surprising moment.
John Mark failed during a missionary journey.
Paul lost confidence in him.
Barnabas did not.
Acts 15 records a sharp disagreement.
Paul and Barnabas separated over Mark.
Many readers focus on the conflict.
I focus on the influence.
Barnabas once again chose restoration.
He once again chose potential.
He once again chose grace.
Years later, Paul would write:
The man Paul once rejected eventually became valuable.
Barnabas saw it before others did.
That is influence.
Real influence is not measured by how many people follow you.
Real influence is measured by how many people continue following Jesus because you refused to give up on them.
The world celebrates platform builders.
Heaven celebrates people builders.
The church desperately needs more Barnabases.
People who encourage instead of crush.
People who restore instead of discard.
People who see evidence of God's work where others only see evidence of someone's past.
People who understand that Christ's blood is powerful enough to rewrite any story.
Maybe today you identify more with Saul than Barnabas.
Maybe your past still follows you.
Maybe old failures still whisper accusations into your mind.
Maybe people remember versions of you that no longer exist.
Listen carefully.
Jesus is not intimidated by your history.
The cross was never a reaction to human goodness.
It was God's answer to human brokenness.
When Jesus cried, “It is finished,” the Greek word was τετέλεσται (tetelestai).
Paid in full.
Completed.
Accomplished.
The debt was settled.
The work was done.
The invitation remains open.
And maybe that is why Barnabas' story matters so much.
Because every believer is living proof that somebody's scandal can become somebody's testimony through the grace of God.
We are all recipients of mercy.
We are all products of redemption.
We are all evidence that Jesus rewrites everything.
So the question is not whether God can transform people.
The question is whether we will believe it enough to become Barnabas-like influences in the lives of others.
Who needs your encouragement today?
Who needs someone to believe God is still working in them?
Who needs a bridge instead of a barrier?
Who needs grace instead of suspicion?
You may never realize how much hangs in the balance.
Neither did Barnabas.
Yet because he chose faith over fear and grace over reputation, the ripple effects continue thousands of years later.
That is influence.
That is discipleship.
That is the Gospel in action.
And perhaps the greatest legacy we can leave behind is not what we accomplish for ourselves, but who we help become everything Christ created them to be.
If this message stirred your heart, do not let it stop here.
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs today.
Because somewhere right now, a future testimony is still trapped inside a present scandal, waiting for someone to believe what Jesus can do.
